title: Ganesha takes dictation
hook: Sam wants a Sanskrit tattoo, and two old ways of honoring holy words
carry: holy words are honored, and understood first
tomorrow: why does Nani start every prayer with om?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna to Arjuna: no one stops acting, so every act can be an offering to God. Today, a best friend's question, and a story about the god who wrote the Mahabharata down.

Sanskrit has a second life on skin: a word for peace on a wrist, om on a shoulder. A best friend wants shanti for graduation and asks, is that okay? Inside Hindu families there isn't one answer, and both answers have roots in one of the best-loved stories about writing. When the sage Vyasa was ready to give the world the Mahabharata, the tradition says, he needed someone who could take it all down. He asked Ganesha.
screen: `SHANTI ON A WRIST?` → `TWO ANSWERS, ONE STORY.` → `VYASA NEEDS A SCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Ganesha agreed, on one condition: Vyasa must never stop dictating, not even for a moment. Vyasa agreed, with a condition of his own: Ganesha must not write a single verse until he understood it. So whenever Vyasa needed a breath, he spoke a verse so knotted that Ganesha had to stop and think. Not every old manuscript has this story, but families everywhere love it, and Ganesha is honored as the epic's scribe. As the god of beginnings, he's there at the first letters too: in Kerala, a child's very first writing often begins with a line to him. Now the two views. The first says: holy words carry the holy. Learning in Hinduism is a goddess, Saraswati, and in many homes books never go on the floor; if a foot brushes one, the hand goes to the book and then to the forehead. On Saraswati's festival, some families lay their books before her. Put om or a name of God on a body, this view says, and where it goes matters: not on a foot, not as a joke. Honor it, or leave it off. The second view says: the same script writes bus signs. Holiness lives in the meaning, held and lived. That's Vyasa's condition: understand it before you write it. Know what it says, and make sure it says it. Notice what both share. Neither treats the letters as decoration.
screen: `GANESHA: NEVER STOP DICTATING.` · `VYASA: UNDERSTAND BEFORE YOU WRITE.` · `ONE VIEW: HOLY WORDS ARE SARASWATI'S.` · `THE OTHER: HOLINESS IS IN THE MEANING.` · `BOTH: NEVER JUST DECORATION.`

segments.voice: If you have a holy book, a prayer card or a page you love nearby, hold it for a moment the way many Hindu homes do, lifted toward the forehead. If not, write one word you'd want to keep. Then read it slowly, the way Ganesha had to, until you're sure what it means. Rest with it, more than ink, for the sit.
Devanagari: one script for holy names and grocery lists alike, and two ways of honoring the holy words it carries.
Your line: holy words are honored, and understood first, on paper or on skin. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Customs vary: in many Hindu homes books are never placed on the floor or stepped over, and a book touched by a foot is touched to the forehead; on Saraswati Puja some families place books before the goddess; at Vidyarambham in Kerala a child's first letters often begin 'Om Hari Sri Ganapataye Namah'. Other families focus on understanding and right use rather than on the written letters themselves.
